periods.activity_title: When Does Nature Become a Resource?
periods.section_anchor: When does Nature become a Resource?

time_bands.activity: Students write on one colour sticky note an element of Nature they interact with daily (river, sunlight, a tree) and on a second colour what humans do with it. Pairs share briefly. Teacher maps contributions onto two columns on the board — 'Nature' and 'Resource' — without yet defining either.

Teacher introduces the chapter's three-condition test: technological accessibility, economic feasibility, cultural acceptability. Students apply each condition to two cases from the text — deep-sea petroleum (technologically inaccessible today) and a tree in a sacred grove (culturally unacceptable to exploit). For each case students write one sentence explaining which condition is unmet and why.

Class constructs a shared working definition: 'An element of Nature becomes a resource when all three conditions are met simultaneously.' Teacher asks: 'If deep-sea drilling technology improves next decade, does that petroleum become a resource? What about the sacred grove tree?' Students discuss in triads, then report conclusions to the class, arguing from the three-condition framework.

Quick written consolidation: each student identifies one element of Nature in their own surroundings, states whether it currently qualifies as a resource, and names the condition that is or is not met. Two or three responses are shared and critiqued by the class before the sitting closes.

periods.section_context: Three-condition test: deep-sea petroleum, sacred grove trees, resource definition
periods.teacher_notes: This opening inquiry builds directly on what students already sense — that Nature surrounds them — and sharpens it into an analytical tool. A common confusion is equating 'resource' with 'useful thing'; clarify that usefulness alone is insufficient if the technological, economic, or cultural condition fails. Invite students to challenge each other's examples to deepen the distinction.

periods.activity_title: Classifying Natural Resources: Use and Renewability
periods.visual_aids: Two-axis classification grid drawn on board: rows = Essential for life / Materials / Energy; columns = Renewable / Non-renewable

time_bands.activity: Teacher draws the two-axis grid on the board. Students read the three use-categories silently from the textbook (essential for life, materials, energy) and list one example they know for each before any class discussion.

Groups of four receive an A3 sheet pre-drawn with the same grid. Teacher calls out twelve resources from the chapter — air, river water, food/cultivated soil, wood, marble, coal, gold, sunlight, wind, petroleum, natural gas, iron — one at a time. Groups place each in a cell with a brief justification. Teacher pauses at coal (appears under both Materials/Energy and Non-renewable) and asks: 'Can one resource sit in two use-columns?' Groups debate and decide.

Groups compare grids with a neighbouring group. Disagreements are brought to the class; teacher facilitates resolution by returning to the textbook's definitions of restoration and regeneration — a fallen tree enriching soil from which new trees grow is the chapter's own illustration of renewability. Students annotate their grids with this example.

Each student writes two sentences: one explaining why sunlight is renewable regardless of how much is used, and one explaining why coal is non-renewable even if there are large reserves. Responses are read aloud and refined as a class.

periods.section_context: Use-categories and renewability axis: air, wood, coal, sunlight, restoration cycle
periods.teacher_notes: Having distinguished Nature from resources in the previous work, students now build a classification system — a tool social scientists use for clearer communication, as the chapter explicitly states. Watch for the common confusion between 'currently available in large quantities' and 'renewable'; coal's 50-year reserve estimate is precisely why it features as a non-renewable even though India has substantial deposits.

periods.activity_title: Nature's Cycles Under Pressure: When Renewal Fails

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes on the board: 'Restoration returns; regeneration creates.' Students read the chapter's tree-decomposition-to-new-tree cycle and in pairs produce a simple two-step diagram — (1) fallen tree decomposes → (2) enriched soil supports new growth — labelling which step is restoration and which is regeneration.

Teacher introduces the chapter's critical condition: renewal holds only when Nature's rhythm is not disturbed. Three disruptions from the chapter are presented one by one — fossil-fuel industrialisation, deforestation, and industrial waste in rivers. For each, students write on an index card: (a) which part of the renewal cycle is broken, (b) one consequence named in the text (e.g., Himalayan glaciers melting faster than precipitation replaces them, threatening water security in the plains).

Class constructs a cause-effect chain on the board: deforestation → reduced transpiration and soil binding → glacier-melt acceleration outpacing precipitation → water insecurity downstream. Teacher asks: 'At what point does a renewable resource effectively behave like a non-renewable one?' Students argue with evidence from the glacier and industrial-waste examples.

Students spend the closing minutes completing the chapter's student activity: each identifies one action in their own surroundings — household, school, or locality — that disrupts a natural renewal cycle and notes what cycle it breaks. Two examples are shared aloud.

periods.section_context: Restoration-regeneration cycle, glacier melt, industrial waste, renewal rhythm
periods.teacher_notes: Having categorised resources by renewability, students now interrogate what renewability actually requires — an undisturbed natural rhythm. A frequent confusion is treating 'renewable' as unconditional; the glacier-melt example in the chapter is the sharpest counter-case, and pressing students to explain at what rate of disturbance a renewable crosses into effective non-renewability builds the analytical edge this section demands.

periods.activity_title: Where Are Resources? Mapping Distribution and Its Consequences
periods.section_anchor: Distribution of Natural Resources and its Implications
materials: Textbook Chapter 1 (mineral distribution map of India)
Outline map of India (one per student)
periods.visual_aids: Mineral distribution map of India from the textbook showing coal, oil, iron ore, and bauxite concentrations

time_bands.activity: Students open the textbook's mineral distribution map. Using four colours, each student marks the concentration zones of coal, oil, iron ore, and bauxite on their outline map, adding a legend. Teacher circulates, checking that students are reading the source map rather than guessing from memory.

Teacher asks three questions drawn from the chapter, answered in writing by each student: (1) Which two mineral resources share overlapping concentration zones — and what industries might develop there? (2) The chapter states industries near resource deposits create local employment but also displacement and environmental damage — choose one mineral from your map and explain both effects. (3) Why does uneven distribution generate trade between regions rather than self-sufficiency?

Class turns to the Kaveri river dispute. Teacher reads aloud the chapter's sentence on water resources crossing political boundaries generating inter-state tensions. Students identify on their maps where the Kaveri basin lies and name all four sharing parties — Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Puducherry. They then write one sentence explaining why shared water differs from shared mineral resources in terms of control and conflict.

Closing analysis: teacher writes on the board 'Wootz steel' and asks what the chapter says about it. Students locate the reference — resources combined with human knowledge and skills generate distinctive trade goods — and write one sentence connecting this to why knowledge is as important as resource location for economic benefit.

periods.section_context: India mineral map, coal-oil-iron-bauxite zones, Kaveri dispute, Wootz steel, trade
periods.teacher_notes: The mineral distribution map is this unit's primary evidence source; students must read it rather than rely on verbal description alone. A common confusion is treating resource location as the sole driver of economic prosperity — the Wootz steel example and the resource curse discussion later in the chapter both complicate this, and the closing question plants that seed deliberately.

competency_edges.competency_text: Identify the spatial distribution of natural resources across India and connect that distribution to trade, human settlements, conflict, and inter-state water disputes.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can interpret a mineral distribution map to correlate resource concentration zones with patterns of trade, industrial settlement, and inter-state conflict.

periods.activity_title: The Paradox of Plenty: The Natural Resource Curse

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes on the board: 'More resources = more wealth.' Students mark a quick agree/disagree on index cards and hold them up. Teacher notes the split and introduces the chapter's term 'paradox of plenty' — regions rich in resources sometimes experience slower economic growth. Students read the relevant paragraph silently.

Teacher poses the analytical question: 'The chapter says resource-rich regions fail when they do not develop industries that convert raw resources into higher-value products. What does that actually mean?' Students work in pairs to construct a concrete chain: raw coal → what must happen → what happens instead in a 'cursed' economy. Pairs share chains; class identifies the missing step — value-converting industry and skilled labour — that India partially avoided through industrial investment.

Students apply the framework to the chapter's Wootz steel example from the Distribution section — iron ore plus metallurgical knowledge produced a globally traded commodity. Then teacher asks: 'If India had exported only raw iron ore, would the same economic benefit have followed?' Students write two sentences arguing why or why not, using the chapter's resource-curse logic.

Structured discussion: 'The chapter says human knowledge, good governance, and strategic planning determine whether resources become lasting benefits or temporary windfalls. Which of these three do you consider most important — and why?' Students make a brief written claim with one piece of evidence from the chapter, then share across the class.

periods.section_context: Paradox of plenty, value-conversion industry, India's industrial investment, governance
periods.teacher_notes: Building on the spatial distribution analysis of resources, this unit pushes students to interrogate whether location alone creates prosperity — the chapter's own answer being no. A common confusion is equating resource abundance with guaranteed economic development; the mechanism of value conversion is the key analytical lever to press.

competency_edges.competency_text: Analyse why resource abundance does not automatically produce economic prosperity, engaging with production, value conversion, and trade.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can analyse the relationship between raw resource extraction, value-converting production, and economic outcomes for resource-rich societies.

competency_edges.competency_text: Identify the spatial distribution of natural resources across India and connect that distribution to trade, human settlements, conflict, and inter-state water disputes.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can connect the geographic concentration of resources to trade advantage and evaluate the conditions under which resource location translates into lasting economic benefit.

periods.section_anchor: Responsible and Wise Use of Natural Resources: Stewardship
materials: Printed or written Bhagavad Gita lokasangraha passage (one per pair)

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes 'stewardship' on the board and asks students to propose a working meaning before reading. Pairs discuss; teacher collects two or three ideas. Students then read the opening of the Stewardship section and refine their definition: acting as responsible custodians of Nature, not owners.

Teacher names the chapter's three consequences of irresponsible resource use — pollution, biodiversity loss, climate change. Students take one consequence each in a group of three, find one specific piece of evidence for it from anywhere in the chapter (glaciers, industrial waste, deforestation), and write a two-sentence explanation of the causal chain from irresponsible use to that consequence.

Pairs receive the lokasangraha passage. Teacher explains the term: acting for the wellbeing of all. Students discuss: 'Does stewardship as defined by the chapter align with lokasangraha? Where does the chapter's argument go beyond individual responsibility?' Each pair produces two bullet points — one alignment and one tension or extension.

Class constructs a shared one-sentence principle of stewardship that combines the chapter's framing with lokasangraha. Teacher records it on the board. Students copy it as the anchor for the subsections that follow in the chapter.

periods.section_context: Stewardship concept, pollution-biodiversity-climate consequences, lokasangraha philosophy
periods.teacher_notes: This unit opens the chapter's stewardship arc, which the subsequent units on groundwater, soil, cement, and the ISA will populate with specific cases. A common confusion is reading stewardship as purely individual — the lokasangraha passage explicitly frames it as collective and governance-level, and the pair task is designed to surface that distinction.

competency_edges.competency_text: Analyse Indian and global conservation efforts and frame the urgency in the context of global climate change, biodiversity loss, and stewardship philosophy.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can construct an argument connecting irresponsible resource use to documented environmental consequences and situate stewardship as both a practical and philosophical imperative.

periods.activity_title: Overexploiting Renewables: Groundwater, Soil, and the Punjab Caselet
periods.section_anchor: Overexploitation of groundwater: a caselet from Punjab
materials: Cause-effect card sets (teacher-prepared: six blank cards per group)

time_bands.activity: Teacher asks: 'The Green Revolution is celebrated for ending food shortages — so what could possibly go wrong with it?' Students predict in writing before any reading. Predictions are noted on the board.

Groups of three read the Punjab caselet and build a six-card cause-effect chain on their desks: (1) shift to high-yielding wheat and paddy varieties → (2) greater water demand than traditional seeds → (3) free electricity supply → (4) over-pumping of groundwater → (5) water table falls below 30 metres in many districts; chemical contamination → (6) short-term food security at cost of long-term sustainability. Each card names the agent, the action, and the consequence. Groups arrange cards in sequence and identify which step was the single most avoidable point of intervention.

Class compares with the soil degradation case: chemical fertilisers and pesticides versus traditional practices — cow dung, mulching, multi-cropping. Students write two sentences: what the traditional practices preserved that industrial inputs destroyed, and what that implies about the definition of 'agricultural progress'.

Students return to the Stewardship section's remedies for groundwater — water harvesting, pond rejuvenation, reduced consumption — and evaluate which of these would have most changed Punjab's trajectory if implemented from the 1960s. Each student writes a one-sentence justified claim.

periods.section_context: Punjab Green Revolution, water table depletion, chemical inputs, soil degradation, remedies
periods.teacher_notes: The Punjab caselet is the chapter's most data-rich case study, connecting the livelihood choices of the Green Revolution to a measurable environmental collapse — 80 per cent overexploited area, water inaccessible above 30 metres. A common confusion is treating the Green Revolution as purely a failure; the chapter explicitly frames it as a trade-off where short-term food security was real, and the analytical task is to evaluate what was exchanged.

competency_edges.competency_text: Correlate agricultural livelihood patterns with natural resource availability and depletion over time.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can trace a causal chain from specific agricultural livelihood choices to measurable depletion of a natural resource and evaluate the sustainability trade-offs involved.

competency_edges.competency_text: Analyse Indian and global conservation efforts and frame the urgency in the context of global climate change, biodiversity loss, and stewardship philosophy.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can evaluate the effectiveness of specific conservation remedies — water harvesting, pond rejuvenation, reduced consumption — against the scale of documented resource depletion.

periods.activity_title: Cement, Vrikshaayurveda, and Sikkim: Alternatives in Practice
materials: Comparison table template (one per student, teacher-drawn on board)
periods.visual_aids: Comparison table on board: rows = Soil management / Pest control / Irrigation / Crop rotation; columns = Industrial approach / Vrikshaayurveda approach / Sikkim outcome

time_bands.activity: Teacher asks: 'What does cement have to do with natural resource stewardship?' Students predict connections. Teacher then reads aloud the chapter's list of cement's harms — fine dust damaging lungs, reducing plant yields, polluting soil and water — and students identify which natural resources are affected.

Students read the Vrikshaayurveda passage and complete the comparison table: for each row (soil management, pest control, irrigation, crop rotation) they write the industrial approach in column 1 and the Vrikshaayurveda approach in column 2. Teacher explains that Vrikshaayurveda was formalised around the 10th century CE as a botanical science — not folklore but a systematised body of knowledge — and asks: 'What does this imply about the assumption that sustainable agriculture is a modern innovation?'

Students read the Pema's farm / Sikkim caselet and add outcomes to column 3 of the table: 100 per cent organic farming by 2016, biodiversity flourishing, 20 per cent average income rise, global model status. Class discusses: 'Which Vrikshaayurveda practices does Sikkim's transition most closely reflect?' Students draw connecting lines across columns.

Each student writes a reflective paragraph (three to four sentences) arguing whether Sikkim's model, if scaled nationally, would constitute evidence that India can avoid the resource curse in agriculture. The argument must use at least two specific details from the section — one from Vrikshaayurveda and one from the Sikkim data.

periods.section_context: Cement pollution, Vrikshaayurveda botanical science, Sikkim organic farming transition, biodiversity
periods.teacher_notes: Having examined over-exploitation cases, students now encounter the chapter's constructive pivot — ancient knowledge and a contemporary state-scale experiment offering evidence that alternatives exist. A common confusion is reading Vrikshaayurveda as merely traditional or informal; the chapter's precision that it was formalised around the 10th century CE as a botanical science is worth underscoring to build students' respect for the depth of the knowledge system.

competency_edges.competency_text: Analyse Indian and global conservation efforts and frame the urgency in the context of global climate change, biodiversity loss, and stewardship philosophy.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can compare industrial and traditional resource-use practices and evaluate the evidence from a documented conservation transition for its scalability and relevance to stewardship goals.

competency_edges.competency_text: Explain India's contributions to sustainable agriculture and renewable energy through ancient knowledge systems and contemporary global leadership.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can explain how an ancient Indian knowledge system addresses contemporary resource-management challenges and assess its continued relevance through a documented modern application.

periods.activity_title: Non-Renewables and the International Solar Alliance
periods.section_anchor: Responsible and judicious use of resources

time_bands.activity: Teacher recaps the chapter's imperative for non-renewables: extend availability until sustainable alternatives emerge. Students write the chapter's coal reserve estimate — approximately 50 more years — and the phrase 'judicious use' on index cards, and in one sentence explain what 'judicious' demands beyond simply using less.

Students read the International Solar Alliance passage. Teacher asks four questions answered in writing: (1) When and by whom was the ISA co-launched? (2) What is the ISA's stated purpose? (3) What does India's investment in solar projects across developing nations indicate about its role in global energy governance? (4) What is the Bhadla Solar Park and what does it exemplify? Students answer individually, then compare with a partner.

Teacher poses the evaluative question: 'The chapter closes by noting that access to clean air and water is inequitably distributed, with the poor bearing disproportionate burdens. How does the ISA address — or fail to address — this inequity?' Students construct a two-column table: 'How ISA helps equity' vs. 'What ISA leaves unaddressed', drawing evidence from the chapter.

Class links the ISA to lokasangraha from the Stewardship section — acting for the wellbeing of all. Students write two sentences arguing whether India's leadership in the ISA is an instance of lokasangraha in international policy, with one piece of evidence from the chapter for their claim.

periods.section_context: ISA co-launch 2015, Bhadla Solar Park, India's solar investment, energy equity, lokasangraha
periods.teacher_notes: Having examined traditional and state-level conservation in the previous unit, students now encounter India's contemporary global leadership in renewable energy. A common confusion is treating the ISA as purely a technical energy initiative; the chapter explicitly frames it in terms of equity and the disproportionate burden on the poor, which connects it to stewardship's ethical dimension.

competency_edges.competency_text: Explain India's contributions to sustainable agriculture and renewable energy through ancient knowledge systems and contemporary global leadership.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can explain India's institutional leadership in global renewable energy governance and evaluate how that leadership connects to domestic and international equity goals.

competency_edges.competency_text: Analyse Indian and global conservation efforts and frame the urgency in the context of global climate change, biodiversity loss, and stewardship philosophy.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can assess an international conservation initiative for its capacity to address both resource sustainability and equitable resource access.

periods.activity_title: Resource Distribution, Conflict, and the Limits of Abundance — A Structured Debate
periods.section_anchor: Distribution of Natural Resources and its Implications
materials: Textbook Chapter 1 (mineral map and Kaveri river material)
Role cards (teacher-prepared: four roles — Karnataka water authority, Tamil Nadu farmers' representative, national water policy adviser, environmental scientist)
periods.visual_aids: Mineral distribution map of India (textbook) projected or displayed for reference during debate

time_bands.activity: Teacher distributes role cards for a structured simulation of a water-sharing negotiation over the Kaveri river. Each student reads their role's brief interest statement (teacher-prepared on the card based on the chapter's content). The four roles are: Karnataka water authority (upstream needs, agricultural demand), Tamil Nadu farmers' representative (downstream irrigation rights), national water policy adviser (inter-state law, equitable sharing), environmental scientist (ecosystem flow requirements). Students with the same role form a cluster and prepare their opening position.

Structured simulation: each role cluster presents a two-minute opening statement grounded in the chapter's content — resource distribution, inter-state tensions, the value of water as a shared resource crossing political boundaries. After all four openings, a five-minute open negotiation follows in which clusters may question each other. Teacher intervenes only to keep arguments anchored to the chapter's evidence.

Debrief out of role: teacher asks the class — 'The chapter says many wars have been fought to control natural resources. What features of the Kaveri dispute make it more likely to end in negotiation than conflict, and what features make conflict possible?' Students write two sentences with evidence from the chapter.

Closing reflection: each student writes one sentence connecting the Kaveri dispute to the chapter's broader claim that uneven distribution shapes not just trade but international and inter-state relations. Two sentences are shared and refined.

periods.section_context: Kaveri river sharing, Karnataka-Tamil Nadu-Kerala-Puducherry dispute, resource conflict, inter-state law
periods.teacher_notes: Having analysed the mineral distribution map analytically in an earlier unit, students now inhabit the human stakes of resource distribution through simulation. The Kaveri dispute is chosen because the chapter names all four parties explicitly and frames it as a live example of how water crossing political boundaries generates tension — students should draw on that framing, not invent facts beyond the chapter.

competency_edges.competency_text: Identify the spatial distribution of natural resources across India and connect that distribution to trade, human settlements, conflict, and inter-state water disputes.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can construct and defend a stakeholder position in a resource dispute by applying evidence about uneven resource distribution and its human and political consequences.

periods.activity_title: Resources, Responsibilities, and Futures: A Whole-Chapter Synthesis
materials: Large sheets of paper or whiteboard space
periods.visual_aids: Blank cause-effect map template on board: central node 'Natural Resource Decision'; branches for Ecological Impact / Economic Outcome / Equity / Governance Response

time_bands.activity: Teacher poses the synthesis question: 'The chapter argues that whether a resource becomes a lasting benefit or a temporary windfall depends on human knowledge, governance, and stewardship. Is that claim supported by the evidence across the whole chapter?' Students individually list, in three minutes, every case or example from the chapter they can recall — three-condition test, mineral map, Kaveri, resource curse, Punjab groundwater, Vrikshaayurveda, Sikkim, cement, ISA, lokasangraha — and mark each with a plus (supports the claim) or minus (complicates it).

Groups of four build a cause-effect map on large paper using the board template: starting from one natural resource decision (each group chooses a different one — mining coal, pumping groundwater, adopting organic farming, launching the ISA), they trace ecological impact, economic outcome, equity consequence, and governance response, citing specific chapter evidence at each branch. Groups must include at least one 'complication' — a place where the chapter's optimistic claim about governance is challenged by evidence.

Gallery: groups post maps and circulate, reading other groups' work. Each student places a star on the branch they find most analytically compelling and a question mark on one they find insufficiently supported by chapter evidence. Groups then have two minutes to respond orally to the question marks they received.

Each student writes a closing argument of three to four sentences answering the synthesis question — the chapter's core claim — using evidence from at least three different sections of the chapter. The argument must reach a conclusion: does the chapter's evidence, taken together, support or complicate the claim that governance and knowledge determine resource outcomes?

periods.section_context: Governance-knowledge-stewardship thesis across mineral maps, Punjab, Sikkim, ISA, lokasangraha
periods.teacher_notes: This synthesis draws together the full arc of the chapter — from the three-condition test defining resources, through spatial distribution and the resource curse, to over-exploitation cases, ancient knowledge systems, and India's global solar leadership. Students should be pressing their own reasoning against the chapter's evidence rather than summarising; the gallery's question-mark step is designed to create that productive friction.

competency_edges.competency_text: Identify the spatial distribution of natural resources across India and connect that distribution to trade, human settlements, conflict, and inter-state water disputes.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can synthesise evidence from mineral distribution, trade patterns, and conflict cases to evaluate the chapter's argument that governance shapes whether resource location produces lasting benefit.

competency_edges.competency_text: Analyse Indian and global conservation efforts and frame the urgency in the context of global climate change, biodiversity loss, and stewardship philosophy.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can integrate conservation cases across Indian traditional knowledge, state-level transitions, and international initiatives to construct a justified position on stewardship's scope and limits.

competency_edges.competency_text: Analyse why resource abundance does not automatically produce economic prosperity, engaging with production, value conversion, and trade.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can integrate evidence about value conversion, governance, and knowledge across multiple chapter cases to evaluate the conditions under which resource wealth produces sustained economic and social benefit.

competency_edges.competency_text: Explain India's contributions to sustainable agriculture and renewable energy through ancient knowledge systems and contemporary global leadership.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can synthesise India's contributions across ancient and contemporary contexts to evaluate the continuity of the stewardship ethic in Indian knowledge and policy.

assessment_items.question_text: Refer to the table provided. A student studying India's mineral distribution notices that coal, iron ore, and bauxite are concentrated in overlapping zones in central and eastern India. Which of the following best explains why industries tend to develop near these overlapping zones rather than near ports?

options.label: A
options.text: Government policy requires all mining companies to build factories within 50 kilometres of their mines.

options.label: B
options.text: Port cities already have too many industries, making inland locations more attractive to investors.

options.label: C
options.text: The central and eastern regions have better climate conditions for industrial workers than coastal areas.

options.label: D
options.text: Transporting heavy raw materials over long distances is costly, so processing near the source reduces production costs.

assessment_items.visual_stimulus:
Mineral | Primary concentration zone | Industries commonly associated
Coal | Jharkhand, Odisha, Chhattisgarh | Steel, power generation
Iron ore | Odisha, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand | Steel, manufacturing
Bauxite | Odisha, Jharkhand, Gujarat | Aluminium smelting
Petroleum | Assam, Gujarat, offshore western coast | Refining, petrochemicals

what_each_option_reveals.B: Confuses market saturation with the chapter's logic of resource-location-driven industrial siting; shows no engagement with transportation cost as the mechanism.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Imports an unsupported climatic variable; the chapter's explanation is economic (extraction and transport costs), not environmental comfort for workers.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Fabricates a regulatory mechanism not present in the chapter; indicates rote recall failure or guessing rather than application of the chapter's cost-logic.

assessment_items.chapter_section: Distribution of Natural Resources and its Implications
assessment_items.question_text: The Kaveri river flows through Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Kerala, and Puducherry. A water-policy adviser argues that inter-state water disputes are fundamentally different from disputes over solid minerals such as coal. Which reasoning best supports this argument?

options.label: A
options.text: Coal is a non-renewable resource, which means all countries protect it more aggressively than water.

options.label: B
options.text: Unlike coal deposits that stay within one region's boundary, river water flows continuously across borders, making exclusive ownership impossible to enforce.

options.label: C
options.text: Water disputes are resolved by geography alone — the state closest to the source always has the greater right.

options.label: D
options.text: Water is less economically valuable than coal, so disputes over it are less intense.

assessment_items.inclusivity: Students unfamiliar with the Kaveri basin may use the chapter's description; the question does not require prior regional knowledge.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Confuses economic value with dispute intensity; the chapter's argument is about political and livelihood stakes, not market price comparison.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Conflates renewability status with diplomatic protection intensity; introduces a claim the chapter does not make and misapplies the non-renewable concept.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Introduces a 'source proximity' rule unsupported by the chapter; likely reflects a commonsense but legally and geographically incorrect assumption students may hold.

assessment_items.question_text: India's coal reserves are concentrated in Jharkhand, Odisha, and Chhattisgarh. Using the chapter's logic, explain two consequences — one economic and one social — that follow from this concentration for the regions where coal is found.
expected_elements: An economic consequence directly connected to resource concentration: industries locating near coal deposits, generating local employment and expanding townships.
A social consequence: either the displacement of people from resource-rich areas OR threats to sacred places OR environmental damage caused by extraction.
A connecting sentence that shows the student understands these as outcomes of uneven spatial distribution, not random events.

assessment_items.chapter_section: Distribution of Natural Resources and its Implications
assessment_items.question_text: The chapter argues that the location of natural resources shapes trade, human settlements, and conflict. Evaluate this claim using at least three pieces of evidence from the chapter — at least one from the mineral distribution map discussion, one from the Kaveri river dispute, and one from the resource curse section.
look_for: A clear evaluative stance — the student agrees, partially agrees, or qualifies the claim and states why.
Specific evidence from the mineral map discussion: concentration zones driving industrial siting, employment, displacement.
Specific evidence from the Kaveri dispute: water crossing political boundaries, four sharing parties, inter-state tension.
Specific evidence from the resource curse: why resource location alone does not guarantee prosperity — value-conversion industry and governance are required.
Integration: the student uses the three pieces together to reach a reasoned conclusion, not as three separate summaries.
Recognition that governance, knowledge, or planning mediates between resource location and outcome — the chapter's nuancing of its own claim.
assessment_items.inclusivity: Students may use bullet-point evidence before writing their evaluation paragraph if that helps them organise their reasoning.

assessment_items.chapter_section: Distribution of Natural Resources and its Implications
assessment_items.task: You are a national water-policy adviser preparing a briefing note on the Kaveri river dispute for a parliamentary committee. Your briefing must map the competing interests of all four parties — Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Kerala, and Puducherry — explain why shared river water generates a different kind of conflict than competition for solid minerals, and recommend one governance principle the chapter's evidence supports for resolving such disputes.
assessment_items.scaffold: Step 1 — Map the parties: For each of the four sharing parties, write one sentence naming their key interest in the Kaveri's water (agriculture, urban supply, ecosystem, etc.). Step 2 — Explain the difference: In two to three sentences, explain why a river flowing across borders creates a different dispute dynamic than, say, coal deposits in one state. Draw on the chapter's logic about resource distribution and conflict. Step 3 — Recommend and justify: State one governance principle (e.g., equitable sharing based on need, environmental flow requirements, joint management body) and use at least one piece of evidence from the chapter — the Kaveri case, the general resource-conflict discussion, or the resource curse argument about governance — to justify why this principle is appropriate.
format_of_output: A three-part written briefing note of approximately 150–200 words, structured as: (1) Party interests table or paragraph, (2) Analysis of dispute type, (3) Governance recommendation with justification.
assessment_items.inclusivity: Students may use a table for Part 1 instead of prose if that helps them organise the four parties' interests before writing the analysis.

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: This task requires students to apply the chapter's spatial-distribution-and-conflict logic to a specific named dispute, adopt a governance perspective, and produce a reasoned recommendation — demonstrating the full Evaluation demand of the LO.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: Step 1 checks factual mapping of the four parties from chapter content. Step 2 is the analytical move — distinguishing flowing water from fixed mineral deposits using the chapter's resource-distribution logic. Step 3 is the evaluative move — selecting and justifying a governance principle with chapter evidence. A student who completes only Step 1 is working at Understanding; only a student who completes and integrates all three reaches Evaluation.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: all four parties named with distinct interests; clear logical distinction between water and mineral dispute dynamics; governance recommendation explicitly tied to chapter evidence. Weak: only two or three parties listed; dispute-type analysis conflates water and minerals; governance recommendation asserted without chapter evidence or lifted verbatim from the text without application.
OPEN_TASK.format_type: Structured discussion prompt with written output
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The briefing-note format is the most natural vehicle for this LO because it requires students to hold multiple stakeholder perspectives simultaneously and synthesise them into a governance recommendation — exactly what 'constructing and defending a stakeholder position' demands. The teacher may substitute a comparison table (comparing parties and dispute features) or a source analysis task if that better suits the class. Any format from the menu that requires multi-party reasoning and a justified conclusion is appropriate.

competency.competency_text: Analyse Indian and global conservation efforts and frame the urgency in the context of global climate change, biodiversity loss, and stewardship philosophy.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can construct an argument connecting irresponsible resource use to documented environmental consequences and situate stewardship as both a practical and philosophical imperative.
assessment_items.chapter_section: Responsible and Wise Use of Natural Resources: Stewardship
assessment_items.question_text: The chapter states that irresponsible treatment of natural resources has caused pollution, biodiversity loss, and climate change, and invokes lokasangraha — acting for the wellbeing of all — as a guiding philosophy. Which of the following best explains why the chapter pairs a practical problem (environmental damage) with a philosophical concept (lokasangraha)?

options.label: A
options.text: Because environmental laws alone have failed, so only religious philosophy can now motivate people to act responsibly.

options.label: B
options.text: Because stewardship requires a motivation that extends beyond individual self-interest to collective wellbeing — which lokasangraha provides as a guiding orientation.

options.label: C
options.text: Because the Bhagavad Gita specifically contains instructions on how to manage mineral resources sustainably.

options.label: D
options.text: Because the chapter is trying to show that ancient Indian philosophy is scientifically equivalent to modern environmental science.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Misreads the chapter's argument as a claim about the failure of law and the sufficiency of religion — the chapter makes neither claim; shows conflation of motivation with institutional failure.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Fabricates a specific textual claim about the Bhagavad Gita's content that is not in the chapter; indicates misreading the role of lokasangraha as content-instruction rather than ethical orientation.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Misunderstands the chapter's intent as one of equivalence-claiming between philosophy and science — the chapter uses lokasangraha as a motivational frame, not a scientific claim.

competency.competency_text: Analyse Indian and global conservation efforts and frame the urgency in the context of global climate change, biodiversity loss, and stewardship philosophy.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can compare industrial and traditional resource-use practices and evaluate the evidence from a documented conservation transition for its scalability and relevance to stewardship goals.
assessment_items.question_text: Sikkim achieved 100 per cent organic farming by 2016, with biodiversity flourishing and farmer incomes rising by an average of 20 per cent. A critic argues that Sikkim's model cannot be scaled to large agricultural states. Which response best uses the chapter's evidence to engage with this criticism?

options.label: A
options.text: The critic is right because the chapter says traditional farming methods are less productive than industrial methods at large scale.

options.label: B
options.text: The critic is wrong because Sikkim proved organic farming always increases income, which any state can replicate.

options.label: C
options.text: The critic raises a legitimate concern; Sikkim is a small state, but the chapter's Vrikshaayurveda principles — soil-appropriate planting, crop rotation, natural pest control — offer scalable practices even if the full transition timeline differs.

options.label: D
options.text: The critic's argument is irrelevant because the chapter says all states should immediately adopt organic farming regardless of scale or context.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Over-generalises from the Sikkim data — the chapter reports outcomes for Sikkim specifically, not as a universal guarantee; shows inability to apply evidence with appropriate scope.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Directly contradicts the chapter's argument; likely a confusion between the chapter's critique of industrial methods and a misread claim of industrial superiority.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Fabricates a prescriptive mandate the chapter does not make; shows replacement of analytical reading with an advocacy misreading.

assessment_items.chapter_section: Responsible and judicious use of resources
assessment_items.question_text: The chapter notes that access to basic resources like clean water and clean air is inequitably distributed, with the poor and pollution-exposed bearing disproportionate burdens. The International Solar Alliance (ISA) focuses on expanding solar energy access. Assess whether the ISA addresses the chapter's equity concern — give one way it does and one way it leaves the concern unresolved.
expected_elements: One specific way the ISA addresses equity: India's investment in solar projects across developing nations expands energy access to lower-income countries that are sunshine-rich but capital-poor.

One specific way the ISA leaves the equity concern unresolved: solar energy access does not directly address the disproportionate burden of air and water pollution on the poor within countries, which requires domestic regulatory action beyond the ISA's mandate.
A connecting sentence that uses the chapter's framing — not a generic equity argument — to anchor both points.

competency.competency_text: Correlate agricultural livelihood patterns with natural resource availability and depletion over time.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can trace a causal chain from specific agricultural livelihood choices to measurable depletion of a natural resource and evaluate the sustainability trade-offs involved.
assessment_items.chapter_section: Overexploitation of groundwater: a caselet from Punjab
assessment_items.question_text: In Punjab, the shift to high-yielding varieties of wheat and paddy during the Green Revolution was accompanied by free electricity supply to farmers. The chapter identifies this combination as a key cause of groundwater depletion. Which of the following best explains the causal mechanism?

options.label: A
options.text: Free electricity attracted factories to Punjab, whose industrial waste contaminated groundwater faster than farming could deplete it.

options.label: B
options.text: High-yielding varieties demanded more water than traditional seeds, and free electricity removed the cost barrier to pumping groundwater without limit.

options.label: C
options.text: High-yielding varieties produced more grain, which required more land, which displaced water bodies and reduced groundwater recharge.

options.label: D
options.text: The Green Revolution reduced rainfall in Punjab by altering the moisture cycle, so groundwater levels fell even without increased pumping.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Confuses land displacement with water demand — the chapter's mechanism is water consumption by the varieties, not land expansion reducing recharge.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Imports the industrial waste mechanism from the rivers section and misapplies it to Punjab groundwater — a within-chapter cross-section confusion.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Introduces a meteorological mechanism (rainfall alteration) not present in the chapter; likely a plausible-sounding but unsupported inference.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can trace a causal chain from specific agricultural livelihood choices to measurable depletion of a natural resource and evaluate the sustainability trade-offs involved.
assessment_items.chapter_section: Overexploitation of groundwater: a caselet from Punjab
assessment_items.question_text: The chapter says Punjab's Green Revolution achieved short-term food security at the cost of long-term sustainability. Which of the following best describes the trade-off the chapter identifies?

options.label: A
options.text: Farmers earned higher incomes in the short term but lost their land to the government when groundwater ran out.

options.label: B
options.text: Food security was achieved nationally but Punjab itself experienced food shortages because it exported all its grain.

options.label: C
options.text: High grain yields in the decades after the Green Revolution were secured by drawing down groundwater reserves that are now inaccessible in many districts and chemically contaminated.

options.label: D
options.text: Traditional seed varieties were lost permanently, so even if water is restored, farmers cannot return to the crops that once sustained them.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Fabricates a land-confiscation consequence not in the chapter; shows the student has the general idea of a cost but cannot locate the chapter's specific mechanism.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Introduces seed loss as the primary trade-off — the chapter mentions chemical contamination and water inaccessibility, not permanent seed extinction, as the primary cost.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Inverts the logic — the chapter's point is that Punjab secured national food supply, not that Punjab went hungry; a confusion between producer and consumer outcomes.

competency.competency_text: Explain India's contributions to sustainable agriculture and renewable energy through ancient knowledge systems and contemporary global leadership.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can explain how an ancient Indian knowledge system addresses contemporary resource-management challenges and assess its continued relevance through a documented modern application.
assessment_items.question_text: Vrikshaayurveda is described in the chapter as an ancient Indian botanical science formalised around the 10th century CE. Which of the following best explains why the chapter introduces Vrikshaayurveda in a section about the problems caused by cement?

options.label: A
options.text: Because both cement's harms and Vrikshaayurveda's practices concern the same resources — soil, water, and plant life — and Vrikshaayurveda offers sustainable alternatives to the industrial inputs that cause those harms.

options.label: B
options.text: Because the 10th century CE is when cement was first introduced to India, and Vrikshaayurveda was the response to its introduction.

options.label: C
options.text: Because the chapter wants to show that ancient knowledge is always superior to modern industrial practices.

options.label: D
options.text: Because Vrikshaayurveda contains ancient instructions specifically for constructing buildings without cement.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Fabricates a construction-specific claim not in the chapter; suggests the student read 'cement section' as meaning 'construction methods' rather than 'industrial pollution'.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Invents a historical causation — cement and the 10th century CE are associated with Vrikshaayurveda's formalisation in the chapter, not cement's introduction; a within-section chronological confusion.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Over-reads the chapter's advocacy as an absolute superiority claim — the chapter calls for learning from traditional practices, not for wholesale replacement of modernity.

competency.competency_text: Explain India's contributions to sustainable agriculture and renewable energy through ancient knowledge systems and contemporary global leadership.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can explain India's institutional leadership in global renewable energy governance and evaluate how that leadership connects to domestic and international equity goals.
assessment_items.chapter_section: Responsible and judicious use of resources
assessment_items.question_text: India and France co-launched the International Solar Alliance (ISA) in 2015. The chapter describes India channelling billions into solar projects across developing nations. Which of the following best explains the significance of targeting developing nations specifically?

options.label: A
options.text: Developing nations are the largest consumers of coal, so switching them to solar will have the greatest immediate impact on global emissions.

options.label: B
options.text: India targets developing nations because it wants to export solar panels and create markets for its own solar industry.

options.label: C
options.text: Many developing nations are sunshine-rich but lack the capital to invest in solar infrastructure, so India's support addresses both the energy access gap and the equity concern the chapter identifies.

options.label: D
options.text: The ISA requires all member nations to purchase solar equipment from India as a condition of receiving funding.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Introduces an emissions-reduction framing the chapter does not use for this specific point; the chapter's focus is energy access and equity, not emissions ranking of developing nations.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Introduces a trade motive not stated in the chapter; reads the ISA through a commercial lens rather than the equity and sustainability lens the chapter applies.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Fabricates a conditionality requirement not present in the chapter; likely a plausible-sounding institutional rule the student invents from general knowledge of international agreements.

competency.competency_text: Analyse why resource abundance does not automatically produce economic prosperity, engaging with production, value conversion, and trade.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can analyse the relationship between raw resource extraction, value-converting production, and economic outcomes for resource-rich societies.
assessment_items.question_text: The chapter describes the 'paradox of plenty' — regions rich in natural resources sometimes experience slower economic growth. Which of the following best identifies the mechanism the chapter uses to explain this paradox?

options.label: A
options.text: International trade agreements force resource-rich developing nations to sell at prices set by wealthier importing countries, keeping growth low.

options.label: B
options.text: Natural resources are exhausted so quickly in rich regions that there is no time to build the infrastructure needed for long-term growth.

options.label: C
options.text: Regions that export raw resources without developing industries to convert them into higher-value products miss the economic gains that value-addition creates.

options.label: D
options.text: Resource-rich regions attract too many migrants, increasing competition and reducing wages below sustainable levels.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Introduces a labour-market competition mechanism not present in the chapter's resource-curse explanation; likely drawn from general economic knowledge rather than the chapter's own argument.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Conflates rapid depletion with the chapter's mechanism — the resource curse is about failure to build value-converting industry, not about speed of exhaustion per se.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Imports an international trade-agreement mechanism not stated in this section of the chapter; may reflect external knowledge of global trade debates that the student applies incorrectly here.

competency.competency_text: Analyse why resource abundance does not automatically produce economic prosperity, engaging with production, value conversion, and trade.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can integrate evidence about value conversion, governance, and knowledge across multiple chapter cases to evaluate the conditions under which resource wealth produces sustained economic and social benefit.
assessment_items.question_text: The chapter says India has generally avoided the resource curse through investment in industrial development, but that balancing extraction with sustainability remains a challenge. Wootz steel — produced from Indian iron ore using advanced metallurgical knowledge — is cited as an example of value conversion. Which of the following best evaluates the completeness of the chapter's claim about India avoiding the resource curse?

options.label: A
options.text: The claim is fully supported because Wootz steel proves India always converts resources into high-value products.

options.label: B
options.text: The claim is irrelevant because the resource curse only applies to oil-producing nations, not countries with diverse mineral resources.

options.label: C
options.text: The claim is partially supported: India developed value-converting industries, but the Punjab groundwater case shows that extraction has sometimes outpaced sustainable planning, suggesting the curse is not fully avoided.

options.label: D
options.text: The claim is unsupported because India exports most of its minerals as raw materials rather than finished goods.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Over-reads a single historical example as universal proof — the chapter's own qualifier ('generally avoided', 'remains a challenge') is ignored, indicating incomplete reading.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Contradicts the chapter's explicit statement that India has invested in industrial development; likely projects general world-knowledge about developing-nation resource exports onto India without reading the chapter's specific claim.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Misidentifies the resource curse as oil-specific — the chapter applies it broadly to resource-rich regions and explicitly discusses India's coal and mineral base; a definitional confusion.
